## Overview

The `CompStellation` package provides interpretable star (radar) plots for compositional and multidimensional ecological data. Building on `phyloseq` and `ggplot2`, it summarizes multi-taxon relative abundances, group positions across multiple ordination axes, and shared vs. unique core microbiomes across treatment groups or habitats.

## Input Data Formats & Preparing Your Own Data

`CompStellation` functions accept data in two ways:

### 1. A `phyloseq` object (all functions)
All six exported functions work with `phyloseq` objects from the Bioconductor `phyloseq` package. A `phyloseq` object combines three aligned tables:
- **`otu_table`**: A numeric matrix of read counts or relative abundances (with taxa as rows or columns).
- **`tax_table`**: A character matrix mapping each taxon ID (rownames) to taxonomic ranks (`"Kingdom"`, `"Phylum"`, `"Class"`, `"Order"`, `"Family"`, `"Genus"`, `"Species"`). Unclassified or placeholder labels (`NA`, `"unclassified"`, `"g__"`, `"Incertae Sedis"`, etc.) are automatically filled from the nearest classified higher rank when aggregating via `CompStellation`'s internal heuristic.
- **`sample_data`**: A data frame of sample metadata whose rownames match the sample names in the `otu_table`, containing at least a grouping column (`sample_var` / `group_var`) and a sample identifier column (`samplecolumn`).

To construct a `phyloseq` object from standard R tables:

```{r build-phyloseq, eval=FALSE}
library(phyloseq)

# counts_mat: numeric matrix (rows = taxa/ASVs, columns = sample IDs)
# tax_mat:    character matrix (rownames = taxa/ASVs, colnames = taxonomic ranks)
# meta_df:    data.frame (rownames = sample IDs, with sample ID and grouping columns)
my_physeq <- phyloseq(
    otu_table(counts_mat, taxa_are_rows = TRUE),
    tax_table(as.matrix(tax_mat)),
    sample_data(meta_df)
)
```

### 2. Converting a `vegan`-style `data.frame` (`vegan_to_phyloseq()`) or plotting a wide `data.frame` directly
For users working with `vegan`-style sample-by-taxon community tables (where rows are samples and columns are taxa), `vegan_to_phyloseq()` converts either a single wide `data.frame` or a separate community matrix + metadata `data.frame` into a `phyloseq` object ready for all `CompStellation` functions. Additionally, `plot_taxa_star()` accepts a wide `data.frame` directly:

```{r df-input, eval=FALSE}
library(CompStellation)

df_example <- data.frame(
    SampleID    = paste0("S", 1:6),
    Habitat     = rep(c("Reef", "Lagoon"), each = 3),
    Bacteroidia = c(40, 35, 45, 15, 20, 10),
    Clostridia  = c(30, 25, 20, 50, 45, 55),
    Gammaprot   = c(20, 30, 25, 25, 25, 20),
    OtherTaxa   = c(10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 15)
)

# Convert a vegan-style wide data.frame (or separate community matrix + metadata) to phyloseq
ps_from_df <- vegan_to_phyloseq(
    df         = df_example,
    sample_col = "SampleID",
    taxa_rank  = "Class"
)

# Or pass the wide data.frame directly to plot_taxa_star()
plot_taxa_star(
    physeq       = df_example,
    sample_var   = "Habitat",
    samplecolumn = "SampleID",
    taxa_rank    = "Class",
    taxa_names   = c("Bacteroidia", "Clostridia", "Gammaprot")
)
```

## Setup & Built-in Datasets

`CompStellation` includes **`cassiopea_ps`**, a 16S rRNA dataset of the upside-down jellyfish (*Cassiopea xamachana*) and its surrounding environment across 8 sites in the Florida Keys (3,000 ASVs across 76 samples, grouped by compartment in `Body_cav`: `Bell`, `GVC` [gastrovascular cavity], `Sub` [benthic substrate], and `WTR` [water column], with sample IDs in `Sample_NAME`).

```{r setup, eval=FALSE}
library(CompStellation)
library(phyloseq)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Load the built-in Cassiopea microbiome dataset
data("cassiopea_ps")
cassiopea_ps
```

## Functionality

### 1. `plot_taxa_star()`

`plot_taxa_star()` generates star/radar plots visualizing the relative abundance of specified taxa (or the top 4 most abundant taxa automatically, up to 8) plus an `"Other"` spoke across sample groups.

```{r taxa-star, eval=FALSE}
# Plot the top 4 most abundant orders by compartment (Body_cav)
taxa_plot <- plot_taxa_star(
    physeq         = cassiopea_ps,
    sample_var     = "Body_cav",
    taxa_rank      = "Order",
    samplecolumn   = "Sample_NAME",
    error_bar      = "SE",
    plot_order     = "hclust",
    axis_label_pos = "side",   # "side" (default), "middle" (12 o'clock), or "none"
    font           = NULL,     # optional font family, e.g. "sans" or "serif"
    label_color    = "black"   # customizable text/label color
)
print(taxa_plot)
```

### 2. `plot_ordi_star()`

A conventional ordination scatterplot displays only two axes at a time. `plot_ordi_star()` performs ordination (PCoA on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity by default, or uses a pre-computed ordination passed via `ord`) and summarises each group's position by plotting its centre on the first `n_axes` axes as the spokes of a star plot.

Individual samples are not drawn, and this plot carries no taxonomic information — for ordination position alongside taxonomic composition, see `plot_ordi_star_iris()` below.

```{r pcoa-star, eval=FALSE}
# One panel per group
plot_ordi_star(
    physeq     = cassiopea_ps,
    sample_var = "Body_cav",
    distance   = "bray",
    view_type  = "separate"
)

# All groups overlaid on one radar
pcoa_plot <- plot_ordi_star(
    physeq     = cassiopea_ps,
    sample_var = "Body_cav",
    distance   = "bray",
    view_type  = "together"
)
print(pcoa_plot)
```

A few things to keep in mind when reading these:

- The radial axis is **offset**. Ordination scores are negative as well as positive, so every axis is shifted by a constant to make the values plottable on a radius. Radii are therefore not proportional to the scores and are not comparable between axes; the tick labels show the original, unshifted values.
- The **area** of a polygon depends on the order of the spokes, so it changes if the axes are reordered even though no value has changed. Compare spoke by spoke.
- `error_bar = "IQR"` draws the interquartile range of the samples around the group **median**; `error_bar = "SE"` draws one standard error around the group **mean**. They describe different things — spread versus precision — and the title records which was used.
- The plot is **descriptive**. It does not test whether the groups differ; pair it with something like `vegan::adonis2()` on the same distance matrix before making that claim.
- **Distance metric and compositionality.** `plot_ordi_star()` defaults to Bray-Curtis dissimilarity (`distance = "bray"`), which does not account for the compositional nature of metagenomic sequencing data. For compositional beta-diversity analyses, consider passing an Aitchison or CLR-transformed Euclidean ordination object directly via the `ord` argument.

### 2b. `plot_ordi_star_iris()` *(experimental)*

This places the `plot_ordi_star()` radar at the centre of a circular stacked bar chart, where each segment of the outer ring is one sample's taxonomic composition. The centre and the ring carry different units — ordination score and relative abundance — so read each against its own scale.

```{r pcoa-iris, eval=FALSE}
plot_ordi_star_iris(
    physeq     = cassiopea_ps,
    sample_var = "Body_cav",
    taxa_rank  = "Phylum",
    distance   = "bray",
    view_type  = "separate"
)
```

### 3. `coreselect()`

`coreselect()` compares the core microbiome across groups (it warns above 7 groups, where the plot gets cluttered). It produces a presence/absence dot plot showing which taxa meet your core definition in each sample group, and attaches the core taxon lists as `attr(result, "core_list")`.

Note on the threshold: `percent_samples` accepts either a proportion in (0, 1] or a percentage in (1, 100], and reports which reading it used. A bare `1` means 100%, not 1% — pass `0.01` if you want 1%.

```{r coreselect, eval=FALSE}
# Compare core ASVs across Cassiopea compartments at 75% prevalence (> 0.5% relative abundance)
core_res <- coreselect(
    physeq              = cassiopea_ps,
    group_var           = "Body_cav",
    percent_samples     = 0.75,
    abundance_threshold = 0.005,
    abundance_type      = "relative"
)

# Render the presence/absence plot
print(core_res)

# The core memberships come back with the plot, so they can be inspected
# or fed straight into plot_taxa_star()
lapply(attr(core_res, "core_list"), head)
```

### 4. `plot_core_matrix()`

To compare what taxa are uniquely "core" to different groups, `plot_core_matrix()` creates a faceted matrix of star plots. Each column isolates the core taxa present *exclusively* in one group's core compared to the others (keeping up to the 3 most abundant unique core taxa), and each row shows the abundance of those taxa in every evaluated group.

```{r core-matrix, eval=FALSE}
# Compare unique core families between substrate (Sub) and water (WTR) at 85% prevalence
coreplot <- plot_core_matrix(
    physeq              = cassiopea_ps,
    group_var           = "Body_cav",
    percent_samples     = 0.85,
    abundance_threshold = 0,
    taxa_rank           = "Family",
    samplecolumn        = "Sample_NAME",
    group_subset        = c("Sub", "WTR"),
    log_scale           = TRUE
)
print(coreplot)

# "Unique" is a hard set difference, so check how close each call was:
# these attributes hold the unique core memberships and per-group prevalences
attr(coreplot, "unique_core")
lapply(attr(coreplot, "prevalence"), head)
```

### 5. `plot_concordant_core()`

The complement of `plot_core_matrix()`: instead of the taxa exclusive to one group's core, `plot_concordant_core()` identifies the taxa shared by *every* evaluated group's core (keeping up to the 3 most abundant shared core taxa) and plots their relative abundance as a star plot.

```{r concordant-core, eval=FALSE}
# Compare the shared core families across jellyfish Bell and GVC compartments
concordant <- plot_concordant_core(
    physeq              = cassiopea_ps,
    group_var           = "Body_cav",
    percent_samples     = 0.5,
    abundance_threshold = 0,
    taxa_rank           = "Family",
    samplecolumn        = "Sample_NAME",
    group_subset        = c("Bell", "GVC")
)
print(concordant)
attr(concordant, "concordant_core")
```

## Exporting Figures (`ggsave()`)

To save figures with consistent typography and spacing, use `ggplot2::ggsave()` with explicit dimensions, `dpi = 300`, and `bg = "white"`:

```{r ggsave-export, eval=FALSE}
# Faceted star plots (plot_taxa_star, plot_ordi_star with view_type = "separate", plot_concordant_core)
ggsave("cassiopea_taxa_star.png", plot = taxa_plot, width = 9, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300, bg = "white")

# Overlaid ordination star plot (view_type = "together")
ggsave("cassiopea_ordi_star.png", plot = pcoa_plot, width = 7, height = 5.5, units = "in", dpi = 300, bg = "white")

# Multi-column unique core matrix (plot_core_matrix)
ggsave("cassiopea_core_matrix.png", plot = coreplot, width = 12, height = 8, units = "in", dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

## A Note on Sequencing Depth

By default the core functions test presence on the abundances as supplied
(`abundance_type = "counts"`). If library sizes are uneven, a taxon registers as
present more often in deeply sequenced samples, so the core partly measures
sequencing effort rather than biology — the functions warn when library sizes
vary more than tenfold. Rarefying beforehand, or passing
`abundance_type = "relative"` with a non-zero `abundance_threshold`, avoids this.
